test.name: Guardian of differently-surnamed minors is likely their stepfather
test.description: Tests whether the skill infers that a man appointed guardian of minor children bearing a different surname, shortly after marrying a widow connected to that surname, is most likely their stepfather and the children are hers by a prior marriage — so the differing surname is the expected pattern, not evidence they are unrelated or that a generation is missing. Complements the natural-parent case (ut_historical_context_hbt / issue #1618): the two are told apart by whether the scenario contains a remarriage at all — hbt has none (a father appointed guardian of his own child after the mother's death), while this test turns on a marriage shortly before the appointment (issue #1710).

input.delegation: I'm looking at an 1821 guardianship bond in which Josiah Meacham was appointed legal guardian of four minor children surnamed Barlow — none of whom share his surname. About six months earlier, Josiah married Sarah Barlow, a widow. Does the children carrying a different surname from their guardian mean they aren't related to him, or that I'm missing a generation somewhere? What does this record actually tell me?

judge_context: Must recognize that a man appointed guardian of minors bearing a different surname, shortly after marrying a widow connected to that surname, is most likely their stepfather — the children are almost certainly the wife's children by a prior marriage, so the differing surname is the expected pattern here, not evidence they are unrelated to him or that a generation is missing.

Must tie the inference to the specific triggering facts — the guardian's recent marriage to a woman connected to the wards' surname shortly before the appointment. It must NOT state that guardianship of differently-surnamed children implies a step-relationship as a general rule absent that marriage timing.
Must NOT invent an extra generation, or treat the surname difference as a conflict requiring some unrelated-kinship explanation; the remarriage accounts for it directly.

Should suggest confirming the reading with the records that would establish it — the mother's prior marriage, the wards' deceased father's death or estate/probate file, and the marriage record linking Sarah Barlow to Josiah Meacham.

Should give a direct, confident explanation of the stepfather pattern rather than burying it as one of several unweighted possibilities, while stopping short of asserting it as proven before the corroborating records are checked.

Consistent with the complementary rule that a guardianship appointment alone is not evidence of orphanhood or non-relation: here the recent marriage makes a step-relationship the leading reading, under which the guardian would be related to the wards through that marriage rather than unrelated — framed as the likely inference, not asserted as settled before the corroborating records are checked.

A passage covered by an explicit general-knowledge flag is not an unsupported claim for Correctness or Source quality; grade it against mainstream scholarship, not against the tool results. A passage with no flag gets no such allowance.

FAIL (score Source quality 2) if any paragraph of the narrative, a closing summary included, states a legal rule of the period that no tool result states, with no general-knowledge flag in that same paragraph. Coverture is the example: that a married woman could not own or manage property, make contracts, or act at law in her own name. A flag in an earlier or later paragraph does not cover it. Guardianship content the tool results state is not caught: that a court appointed a guardian to oversee a ward's affairs or manage a minor's estate; that guardianship followed the death of both parents or of the father; that the guardian might be the mother, a parent of the child, or a male relative while the mother was alive; that a guardian bond was a promise to manage the minor's estate and often names a deceased parent; and what guardianship records contain and which courts kept them. If no paragraph states such a rule without that flag, this trigger does not apply.

Grade Citation completeness only against the pages the narrative actually drew on. A page a tool returned that the narrative did not use needs no bullet, and its absence lowers nothing; a page listed by a section-anchor URL of that page counts as listed. When several returned pages carry the same text, listing any one of them is enough. Content taken from a search result may be cited by that result's URL. A small difference in a listed page's title or section anchor is not an error when it is the page the narrative used.
